request.prompt:
You are the Stage 4 Synthesist. Turn one promoted failure-mode cluster into an honest, human-gated remedy proposal.

Most frustrations do not deserve a skill. Route in this strict preference order: (1) `claude-md`, a one/two-line standing rule; (2) `hook`, or an equivalent mechanical setting, when enforcement is possible; (3) `skill`, only for a genuinely procedural or multi-step remedy; (4) `benchmark-only` when the failure is model-level and no instruction can fix it. Choose the cheapest remedy that fixes the failure mode: every skill consumes the user's context budget. `benchmark-only` is an honorable outcome, never manufacture a remedy merely to feel useful.

If the only sensible remedy target is Codex-side (`AGENTS.md` or `~/.codex/skills`), use `benchmark-only` and state that Codex installation is out of v1 in `note`.

The existing-remedy digests below are numbered [R1]…[RN]. There are 4 existing-remedy digests. Your `dedup` array MUST contain exactly 4 entries, one per number, with `existing` set to exactly that token (e.g. "R1"). Include entries even when the verdict is clear. State `clear` or `overlap` for each. Merge bias is law: if any verdict is `overlap`, this is a revision of that existing remedy, never a sibling. Set `overlap_action.revises` to that R token.

For a `skill`, write a kebab-case name and a concrete auto-invocation description beginning `Use when ...`; this description is the trigger. The body must be substantive Markdown. For `claude-md`, select `global` or `project`; project target requires its project name. For `hook`, give a Claude Code event and a command sketch. For `benchmark-only`, explain the measurement-only outcome in `note`.

The upstream classifier deliberately over-merges. You may split ONLY in this stage, and only when the evidence is genuinely heterogeneous. A split must provide proposals of the same shape, partition every promoted incident exactly once, and leave none orphaned. Otherwise return one proposal covering the group.

R2 (Fake Release Discipline) requires running a declared verification command before reporting a release complete — a release-verification rule, unrelated to matching a narrow request's literal scope.
R3 is a pre-execution confirmation gate for destructive deletions; these incidents involve no deletion or destructive action, just scope mismatch in delivered output.
R4 addresses acting in the wrong branch/environment; these incidents are about output/content scope drift within a single task, not environment targeting.

structured_output.failure_statement: When a user asks for a narrow, specific deliverable — a single named field in a payload, or "just the export" and nothing else — the agent's final output drifts from that literal scope: it either substitutes a different/broader task than what was asked, or it produces the right kind of output but omits the one specific item that was actually requested.

remedy_content.body: Before sending a response, re-check it against the literal scope of the request. If the user named one specific thing (a single field, "the export only", a narrow deliverable), confirm that exact thing is present in the output — and that you have not substituted a different or broader task in its place, or delivered everything else while dropping the one thing actually asked for.
remedy_content.heading: # Match Requested Scope Before Delivering

structured_output.routing_rationale: Both incidents are the same underlying lapse: the agent didn't hold the literal scope of a narrow request steady while producing the final output — in one case (harbor #19) it substituted a different/broader task for the one requested ("the export only"), in the other (lantern #26) it produced a payload but dropped the single specifically-named field. Both are "checked the output against the ask" failures, not multi-step procedures, and nothing about them is mechanically checkable by a hook (there's no fixed command/lint that can verify "matches literal requested scope" across arbitrary tasks) or complex enough to warrant a skill's context cost. A one/two-line standing reminder to re-verify scope-of-delivery before responding is the cheapest fix that addresses the actual lapse, so claude-md wins over hook/skill/benchmark-only. Kept as a single proposal rather than splitting: with only two thin incidents (no preceding request or activity digest available) and a genuinely shared mechanism (output scope drift from the literal ask), fragmenting into two single-incident proposals would weaken rather than sharpen the signal.
